did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with the heading, “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet—according to Shigionoth,” and ends with a musical instruction: “For the director of music, with my stringed instruments.” This presents the chapter as a prayer intended also to be performed with music.

Did you know? Habakkuk asks that God’s work be renewed “in the midst of the years” and made known. Yet alongside his fear, he also asks: “In wrath, remember mercy”—that mercy be remembered in the time of judgment.
Did you know? The revelation is described as God appearing from Teman and Mount Paran. The text presents God’s glory as so great that it covers the heavens, while the earth is filled with his praise.

Did you know? Light plays a central role in the description of the revelation: “His brightness was like the light.” Alongside the light appears the phrase “where his power is hidden,” emphasizing that God’s power is revealed yet also concealed.
Did you know? Pestilence and plague are described as going before God. Thus, the revelation is not merely a spectacular sight, but also carries threatening, world-changing power.

Did you know? In the description of the revelation, God “measures” the earth, while the ancient mountains shatter and the age-old hills sink down. All of nature is portrayed as responding to his presence.

Did you know? Habakkuk asks whether the Lord’s anger is directed at the rivers or the sea, and then describes him as riding on horses and chariots of salvation. The same passage later mentions the bow and the oaths made to the tribes.

Did you know? The mountains, the deep, the sun, and the moon all take part in the description of the revelation: the mountains tremble, the deep roars, and the sun and moon are described as standing still.

Did you know? The vision of divine power provokes a severe physical reaction in Habakkuk: his stomach trembles, his lips quiver, and his bones are described as decaying. Even so, he waits for the day of trouble.

Did you know? Verses 17–19 describe a sudden transition from deprivation to joy: even if there are no figs, grapes, olives, crops, sheep, or cattle, Habakkuk says that he will still rejoice in the Lord and find his strength in him. The chapter ends with the words, “For the director of music, with my stringed instruments.”
